request.text:
name: Desktop release

# Tag-driven release workflow for the Sovereign desktop app.
#
# Trigger:
#   git tag desktop-v0.1.0 && git push origin desktop-v0.1.0
#
# What it does:
#   1. Build matrix across mac arm64 / mac x86_64 / linux x86_64 / windows x86_64.
#   2. Run scripts/fetch-desktop-binaries.sh to stage PaddleOCR models + PDFium.
#   3. `tauri build --config tauri.release.conf.json` — produces installers.
#   4. Upload artifacts to a draft GitHub Release named after the tag.
#
# Code signing is intentionally OFF in v1 (see RELEASING.md §"Code signing").
# Notarization / Authenticode are tracked as Phase 2.

on:
  push:
    tags:
      - "desktop-v*"
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: "Tag to attach the release to (e.g. desktop-v0.1.0). Leave blank to use the workflow ref."
        required: false
  # Callable by the manual "Release (manual)" orchestrator (release.yml). Same
  # contract as cli-release.yml: `inputs.tag` covers dispatch + call; a tag push
  # leaves it empty and the version-check / resolve steps fall back to GITHUB_REF.
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: "Tag to attach the release to (e.g. desktop-v0.1.0)."
        required: false
        type: string
        default: ""

permissions:
  contents: write  # needed to create / upload to a GitHub Release

jobs:
  # Pure, no-inference freshness gate for the pre-built router-embed cache
  # (sovereign/router/router-embed-cache.json), baked into the desktop binary so
  # first launch hits the cache instead of re-embedding ~310 router exemplars
  # (minutes on a CPU-only embed slot). `build` needs this, so a stale cache
  # fails the whole release fast — the suspenders to bump-desktop-version.sh's
  # belt (which regenerates on bump). Cheap: compiles sovereign-core (no llama)
  # and runs one test; no model download, no inference.
  router-cache-gate:
    name: router-cache freshness gate
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          # Build the TAG when called by release.yml's bump flow (the run's
          # own SHA predates the bump commit). Empty on tag pushes → default.
          ref: ${{ inputs.tag }}
      - name: Install Rust toolchain
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
      - name: Cache cargo
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          workspaces: "."
          key: router-cache-gate
          cache-on-failure: true
      # mold + clang: the workspace .cargo/config.toml pins them as the
      # Linux linker — even this "cheap" job's proc-macro build scripts
      # link through ld.mold ("invalid linker name" without it).
      # protoc + libprotobuf: sovereign-core → corpus-engine → LanceDB
      # (lance-encoding's prost-build). No llama in this dep tree, so no
      # cmake/Vulkan needed.
      - name: System deps
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y mold clang protobuf-compiler libprotobuf-dev
      - name: Router embed cache is fresh
        run: cargo test -p sovereign-core --test router_cache_fresh

  build:
    name: build / ${{ matrix.platform.name }}
    needs: router-cache-gate
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.platform.runner }}
    # Execution backstop. A native build here runs ~40 min; 120 bounds a wedged
    # job (esp. the self-hosted Intel leg) so it can't sit for the 6h default.
    # NB: this caps RUN time, not queue wait — a self-hosted leg with its runner
    # offline still queues (manual-start model: start ./run.sh before tagging).
    timeout-minutes: 120
    # Updater signing secrets (TAURI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY +
    # TAURI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD) are scoped to the `prod`
    # environment, so the job must claim it to access them. Without
    # this line, secrets.TAURI_UPDATER_* resolve to empty strings and
    # Tauri's bundler silently skips producing .sig sidecars,
    # breaking the updater chain.
    environment: prod
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        platform:
          # 2026-06-19: Linux + macOS-arm64 are both validated by local
          # rehearsals from current HEAD — Linux via a native toolbox build of
          # the .deb + .AppImage; macOS-arm64 via scripts/build-desktop-macos.sh
          # producing the deep-ad-hoc-signed .app + a verified .dmg. The Tauri
          # build step below now self-heals the one local-vs-CI difference: when
          # create-dmg's Finder/osascript cosmetic step is unavailable it
          # packages the DMG from the signed .app via hdiutil (see that step).
          # macOS-x86_64 + Windows stay commented until each is built and
          # verified locally — pushing untested legs previously drained the
          # Actions budget.
          #
          # macOS Intel (x86_64): NATIVE self-hosted runner — labels
          # [self-hosted, macOS, X64] (decided 2026-06-20, superseding the brief
          # arm64-only drop). GitHub's hosted `macos-13` Intel runner is RETIRED:
          # the job hung forever on "Waiting for a runner to pick up this job:
          # macos-13" and, since publish is `needs: build`, blocked the whole
          # release. CROSS-compiling x86_64 on a macos-14 (arm64) runner proved
          # too fragile — cross-only link blockers a native build never hits
          # (llama.cpp cpp-httplib→OpenSSL; lance AVX-512 SIMD kernels). So the
          # leg targets a real Intel Mac, which built + ran clean from this HEAD
          # on 2026-06-20 (signed x64 .dmg, dyld-verified). MANUAL-start model:
          # start the runner (`./run.sh`) BEFORE pushing a desktop-v* tag, or
          # this leg queues waiting for it. publish is now decoupled
          # (`if: !cancelled()`), so a FAILED/absent Intel build no longer sinks
          # the arm64 + Linux artifacts the way macos-13 did. See RELEASING.md
          # §"macOS Intel (x86_64) — self-hosted runner" for the per-release flow.
          #
          # WINDOWS: code is wired (sovereign-inference cfg(target_os="windows")
          # llama arm, CPU baseline + feature-selected vulkan/cuda; readiness
          # fixes landed) and the Rust/cfg layer cross-checks clean via
          # scripts/windows-crosscheck.sh (cargo-xwin). IMPORTANT: windows-2022 is
          # a NATIVE x86_64 runner — that build is NOT cross-compiled, so the
          # OpenSSL/lance cross-link failures above are cargo-xwin (cross)
          # ARTIFACTS that should not occur there. cargo-xwin cannot prove the
          # native-dep build; the leg stays COMMENTED until the NATIVE build is
          # validated on a Windows VM or one windows-2022 run. If native Windows
          # DOES hit the llama OpenSSL link, the minimal fix is dropping `mtmd`
          # from the desktop (no common → no cpp-httplib → no OpenSSL), not a
          # vendored fork. Backend roadmap: CPU first, then windows-x64-vulkan
          # (--features windows-vulkan + Vulkan SDK).
          - name: macos-arm64
            runner: macos-14
            target: aarch64-apple-darwin
          - name: macos-x86_64
            # NATIVE Intel via a self-hosted runner (see the matrix note above).
            # runs-on accepts this label array; the registered Intel Mac matches
            # all three. Start `./run.sh` before tagging — manual-start model.
            runner: [self-hosted, macOS, X64]
            target: x86_64-apple-darwin
          - name: linux-x86_64
            runner: ubuntu-22.04
            target: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
          # - name: windows-x86_64           # CPU; uncomment after NATIVE validation (VM or one windows-2022 run)
          #   runner: windows-2022
          #   target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
          # NOTE (2026-07-10): a LOCAL containerized Windows leg exists —
          # scripts/build-desktop-windows.sh (cargo-xwin + NSIS in a native
          # arm64 container; shipped desktop-v0.1.19's x64-setup.exe). The
          # old cross-link blockers are solved there (see that script + the
          # RELEASING.md "Full local release" symptom table); this CI leg
          # stays available as the native-MSVC alternative.
          # - name: windows-x86_64-vulkan     # NVIDIA+AMD+Intel GPU; needs a Vulkan SDK install step + features: windows-vulkan
          #   runner: windows-2022
          #   target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
          #   features: windows-vulkan

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          # Build the TAG when called by release.yml's bump flow (the run's
          # own SHA predates the bump commit). Empty on tag pushes → default.
          ref: ${{ inputs.tag }}

      - name: Verify version consistency
        # Cheap pre-flight: refuse to spend 30+ minutes building a tag whose
        # three version files (Cargo.toml / tauri.conf.json / package.json)
        # disagree. Derives the expected value from the tag itself when it
        # matches desktop-vX.Y.Z; otherwise just checks the three agree.
        shell: bash
        run: |
          ref="${{ inputs.tag }}"
          [ -n "$ref" ] || ref="${GITHUB_REF#refs/tags/}"
          if [[ "$ref" == desktop-v* ]]; then
            expected="${ref#desktop-v}"
            scripts/check-desktop-version.sh "$expected"
          else
            scripts/check-desktop-version.sh
          fi

      - name: Install Rust toolchain
        uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          targets: ${{ matrix.platform.target }}

      # CACHE REF-SCOPING: tag-triggered runs save caches scoped to the tag
      # ref, which no future run can restore — only main-scoped caches are
      # visible to everyone. Release via the manual orchestrator
      # (release.yml, dispatched on main) at least once so this key gets a
      # main-scoped save; from then on every release restores warm. (See the
      # longer note in cli-release.yml.)
      - name: Cache cargo
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2
        with:
          # Single Cargo workspace at the repo root (post-monorepo, 2026-05).
          # Targeting "." picks up the only Cargo.lock/target pair that exists.
          workspaces: "."
          key: desktop-release-${{ matrix.platform.target }}
          # Seed even when a release attempt fails mid-build.
          cache-on-failure: true
      # See ci.yml's test job for the full story: rust-cache's cleanup
      # deletes target/llama-cmake-cache while keeping the sys crate's
      # fingerprint (poisoned cache → link failure). Cache the tree
      # separately; key shared with CI (the C++ is CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
      # regardless of cargo profile). Windows uses a LOCALAPPDATA path
      # instead of this dir; the steps are harmless no-ops there.
      - name: Cache llama.cpp CMake tree
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: target/llama-cmake-cache
          key: llama-cmake-${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}-${{ hashFiles('Cargo.lock') }}
      - name: Guard llama fingerprint vs missing CMake tree
        shell: bash
        run: |
          if ! ls target/llama-cmake-cache/*/lib*/libllama.* >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            rm -rf target/*/.fingerprint/llama-cpp-sys-4-* 2>/dev/null || true
          fi

      - name: Install Tauri CLI
        run: cargo install tauri-cli --version "^2.0.0" --locked

      - name: Setup Node
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "20"
          cache: "npm"
          cache-dependency-path: sovereign/crates/sovereign-desktop/package-lock.json

      - name: Install npm deps
        working-directory: sovereign/crates/sovereign-desktop
        run: npm ci

      - name: Linux system deps (AppImage / .deb + Vulkan backend)
        if: matrix.platform.runner == 'ubuntu-22.04'
        run: |
          # Vulkan build tooling is NOT on the stock ubuntu-22.04 runner
          # and stock Ubuntu apt has no `glslc`/`shaderc`/`spirv-headers`.
          # sovereign-inference forces llama-cpp-4's `vulkan` feature on
          # Linux, so llama-cpp-sys-4 builds ggml with -DGGML_VULKAN=ON and
          # needs: glslc (ggml-vulkan's vulkan-shaders-gen), the SPIR-V
          # headers (ggml-vulkan.cpp #includes <spirv/unified1/spirv.hpp>
          # for the `spv::` namespace), and libvulkan.so to link against.
          # LunarG's apt repo provides all three. (Mirrors
          # containerfiles/Containerfile.linux-build — keep them in sync.)
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg
          curl -fsSL https://packages.lunarg.com/lunarg-signing-key-pub.asc \
            | sudo tee /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/lunarg.asc >/dev/null
          curl -fsSL https://packages.lunarg.com/vulkan/lunarg-vulkan-jammy.list \
            | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/lunarg-vulkan-jammy.list >/dev/null
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y \
            libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev \
            libappindicator3-dev \
            librsvg2-dev \
            patchelf \
            libfuse2 \
            squashfs-tools \
            mold \
            protobuf-compiler libprotobuf-dev \
            libvulkan-dev vulkan-headers spirv-headers spirv-tools shaderc
          # protobuf-compiler (protoc) + libprotobuf-dev (the well-known
          # protos, e.g. google/protobuf/empty.proto) are required by
          # lance-encoding's prost-build step. NOT preinstalled on the
          # current ubuntu-22.04 runner image (GitHub slimmed it) — the
          # build dies in lance-encoding with "Could not find `protoc`"
          # without them.
          # `mold` is required by .cargo/config.toml's
          # x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu rustflags. Without it, every
          # crate's link step errors with
          # `clang: error: invalid linker name in argument '-fuse-ld=mold'`.
          # The repo's config is keyed on linker speed for local dev;
          # CI just needs the binary on PATH.
          #
          # AppImage bundling also shells out to xdg-mime /
          # glib-compile-schemas / gdk-pixbuf-query-loaders / rsvg-convert;
          # the runner image already ships those (xdg-utils, libglib2.0-bin,
          # libgdk-pixbuf2.0-bin, librsvg2-bin). The minimal build container
          # installs them explicitly — see the Containerfile.

      - name: macOS build deps (lld, protobuf, cmake, SDKROOT)
        # Match on the TARGET, not the runner: the self-hosted Intel leg's
        # `runner` is a label ARRAY ([self-hosted, macOS, X64]), so the old
        # `startsWith(runner, 'macos')` was false for it and silently skipped
        # this step. Both macOS legs carry a `*-apple-darwin` target.
        if: contains(matrix.platform.target, 'apple-darwin')
        env:
          # Stop brew's 30-day auto-cleanup from firing mid-install. On a
          # self-hosted Mac it can trip over pre-existing root-owned files under
          # /usr/local (observed 2026-06-20: a python pycache perm-denied aborted
          # the whole `brew install` even though the formula installed fine).
          HOMEBREW_NO_INSTALL_CLEANUP: "1"
          HOMEBREW_NO_ENV_HINTS: "1"
        run: |
          # Self-hosted runners launched via ./run.sh inherit a MINIMAL PATH that
          # may lack Homebrew. Source its shellenv so `brew` + its installed
          # tools (lld, protoc) resolve, and persist the bin dir to later steps
          # via $GITHUB_PATH. Intel Macs use /usr/local; the /opt/homebrew branch
          # is the Apple-Silicon fallback. No-op on GitHub-hosted runners (brew
          # is already global there).
          if [ -x /usr/local/bin/brew ]; then
            eval "$(/usr/local/bin/brew shellenv)"
            echo "/usr/local/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
            echo "/usr/local/sbin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
          elif [ -x /opt/homebrew/bin/brew ]; then
            eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"
            echo "/opt/homebrew/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
          fi
          # lld: .cargo/config.toml's *-apple-darwin rustflags pass
          # `-fuse-ld=lld`, which clang routes to LLVM's lld. The hosted macos-14
          # runner doesn't ship lld; the Homebrew LLVM formula provides it.
          #
          # protobuf: lance-encoding's build script runs prost-build, which
          # shells out to `protoc`. None of the runners ship it (the Linux
          # job installs protobuf-compiler explicitly via apt) — without this
          # the build dies in lance-encoding with "Could not find `protoc`".
          #
          # cmake: llama-cpp-sys-4 needs it to compile llama.cpp's Metal backend.
          # Preinstalled on the hosted macOS runner, but NOT guaranteed on a
          # self-hosted Mac — install it explicitly (brew skips it if present).
          brew install lld protobuf cmake
          # SDKROOT: llama-cpp-sys-4's bindgen step resolves system headers via
          # the macOS SDK; without an explicit SDKROOT it fails with
          # "'memory' file not found". $GITHUB_ENV persists it to every later
          # step (this run: shell is otherwise discarded). See
          # feedback_macos_sdkroot_for_bindgen.
          echo "SDKROOT=$(xcrun --show-sdk-path)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          # The macOS deployment target is pinned on the Tauri build step's
          # own `env:` block (below), not here. ggml-backend-dl.cpp uses
          # std::filesystem (needs 10.15); with MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET unset,
          # the `cc` crate falls through to the Xcode SDK's DefaultDeploymentTarget
          # (10.13 on Xcode 15.4) and the C++ compile fails. The repo's
          # .cargo/config.toml [env] also force-sets it (covers local + non-CI),
          # but a step-level env: is the most direct guarantee it reaches the
          # build-script process here.

      - name: Windows build deps (protoc)
        if: matrix.platform.runner == 'windows-2022'
        shell: pwsh
        run: |
          # Same protoc need as macOS: lance-encoding's build script runs
          # prost-build, which shells out to `protoc`. The windows-2022 runner
          # does not ship it; without this the build dies in lance-encoding
          # with "Could not find `protoc`". choco's package installs the full
          # protoc distribution (binary + include/google/protobuf well-known
          # protos) and drops a shim in C:\ProgramData\chocolatey\bin, which is
          # already on PATH — so the later build step resolves it with no extra
          # PATH wiring. (Linux installs protobuf-compiler + libprotobuf-dev
          # via apt; macOS gets protobuf via brew.)
          choco install protoc -y --no-progress

      # OCR is PaddleOCR (in-process ONNX) as of 2026-05-27 — no tesseract
      # to install/stage. The fetch script pulls the PaddleOCR models +
      # PDFium for the target triple. (Tesseract remains a code fallback but
      # is no longer bundled; see RELEASING.md §"External binaries".)
      - name: Stage OCR assets (PaddleOCR models + PDFium)
        shell: bash
        run: scripts/fetch-desktop-binaries.sh ${{ matrix.platform.target }}

      - name: Tauri build
        working-directory: sovereign/crates/sovereign-desktop
        shell: bash
        env:
          # AppImage tooling (linuxdeploy + its appimage plugin) ship as
          # AppImages themselves; force extract-and-run so they never depend on
          # a FUSE mount. Harmless on a FUSE-capable runner, and it was the
          # proven fix when the nested appimage plugin couldn't mount during a
          # local container rehearsal (2026-06-19). No effect on non-Linux jobs.
          # (Paired with squashfs-tools in the Linux deps step, which provides
          # the mksquashfs appimagetool calls to pack the final image.)
          APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN: "1"
          # macOS deployment target floor for ggml's std::filesystem use
          # (ggml-backend-dl.cpp needs 10.15). Setting it on this step's env
          # puts it in the cargo-tauri → cargo → build-script process tree, so
          # the `cc` crate reads it (step 1) instead of falling through to the
          # Xcode SDK default of 10.13. Harmless on Linux/Windows runners.
          MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET: "10.15"
          # tauri-bundler signs each updater artifact in-place and writes a
          # .sig file next to it when these are present. Without them, the
          # bundle still builds but no signatures are produced, and the
          # updater plugin will reject any manifest pointing at it. Set
          # these in repo Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions.
          # See RELEASING.md "Auto-updates" for the keypair generation flow.
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TAURI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.TAURI_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          # ggml/llama are static-linked into the binary (the vendored
          # llama-cpp-4 drops `dynamic-link` from its defaults), so the
          # bundle is self-contained — no libggml*.so / libllama*.so to
          # locate or co-package, and linuxdeploy's AppImage dependency walk
          # only sees packageable system libs (libvulkan.so.1, GTK, …). A
          # single build pass produces all installers.
          #
          # Capture the real exit code (don't pipe — a pipeline's status is the
          # last stage's, which would mask a failed build as success).
          set +e
          cargo tauri build \
            --target ${{ matrix.platform.target }} \
            --config src-tauri/tauri.release.conf.json
          BUILD_RC=$?
          set -e
          if (( BUILD_RC == 0 )); then exit 0; fi
          # The one local-vs-CI difference we tolerate: macOS create-dmg's
          # osascript step needs to drive Finder (Apple Events); if the runner
          # can't, bundle_dmg.sh exits 64 with the .app already built + signed.
          # Package the DMG from that .app via hdiutil — functionally identical,
          # minus the background image. Mirrors scripts/build-desktop-macos.sh.
          # ANY other failure (or non-macOS) re-raises the original exit code.
          BUNDLE="$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle"
          # .app name tracks productName in tauri.conf.json ("svrnmesh" since
          # the 2026-06-29 rename) — glob so a rename can't silently disable
          # this fallback (which is what happened locally for v0.1.19).
          APP="$(find "$BUNDLE/macos" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.app' -print -quit 2>/dev/null || true)"
          APP_NAME="$(basename "${APP:-svrnmesh.app}" .app)"
          if [[ "${RUNNER_OS:-}" == "macOS" && -n "$APP" && -d "$APP" ]] && ! ls "$BUNDLE"/dmg/*.dmg >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "Tauri DMG step failed but the signed .app exists — packaging via hdiutil (create-dmg's Finder step was unavailable)."
            VERSION="$(/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :CFBundleShortVersionString' "$APP/Contents/Info.plist")"
            case "${{ matrix.platform.target }}" in
              aarch64-apple-darwin) ARCH_SUFFIX=aarch64 ;;
              x86_64-apple-darwin)  ARCH_SUFFIX=x64 ;;
              *)                    ARCH_SUFFIX="$(uname -m)" ;;
            esac
            DMG_OUT="$BUNDLE/dmg/${APP_NAME}_${VERSION}_${ARCH_SUFFIX}.dmg"
            rm -f "$BUNDLE"/macos/rw.*.dmg
            STAGE="$(mktemp -d)"
            ditto "$APP" "$STAGE/$APP_NAME.app"        # preserves the ad-hoc signature
            ln -s /Applications "$STAGE/Applications"   # drag-to-install target
            mkdir -p "$BUNDLE/dmg"
            hdiutil create -volname "$APP_NAME" -srcfolder "$STAGE" -fs HFS+ -format UDZO -ov "$DMG_OUT"
            rm -rf "$STAGE"
            echo "DMG built via hdiutil fallback: $DMG_OUT"
          else
            echo "::error::Build failed (exit $BUILD_RC) and it is not the macOS Finder/TCC DMG cosmetic case — see the cargo output above." >&2
            exit "$BUILD_RC"
          fi

      - name: Arch-qualify macOS updater artifacts
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        shell: bash
        run: |
          # Tauri emits the macOS updater archive as a bare
          # `<productName>.app.tar.gz` (+ .sig) — identical names across the
          # two mac targets, which would collide in the publish job's flatten
          # step and can't carry the arch the updater manifest endpoint
          # (landing/api/desktop/updater.js) matches on. Rename to
          # `<productName>_<ver>_<aarch64|x64>.app.tar.gz`. Renaming is safe:
          # the .sig signs the tar.gz BYTES, and the manifest inlines the sig
          # content while pointing at the renamed asset URL.
          BUNDLE="$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/macos"
          case "${{ matrix.platform.target }}" in
            aarch64-apple-darwin) ARCH_SUFFIX=aarch64 ;;
            x86_64-apple-darwin)  ARCH_SUFFIX=x64 ;;
            *)                    ARCH_SUFFIX="$(uname -m)" ;;
          esac
          shopt -s nullglob
          for f in "$BUNDLE"/*.app.tar.gz; do
            base="$(basename "$f" .app.tar.gz)"
            # already qualified (idempotent re-runs)
            [[ "$base" == *"_${ARCH_SUFFIX}" ]] && continue
            VERSION="$(/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy -c 'Print :CFBundleShortVersionString' "$BUNDLE/$base.app/Contents/Info.plist")"
            mv "$f" "$BUNDLE/${base}_${VERSION}_${ARCH_SUFFIX}.app.tar.gz"
            if [[ -f "$f.sig" ]]; then
              mv "$f.sig" "$BUNDLE/${base}_${VERSION}_${ARCH_SUFFIX}.app.tar.gz.sig"
            fi
          done
          ls -la "$BUNDLE"

      - name: Upload artifacts
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: desktop-${{ matrix.platform.name }}
          # Cargo's workspace target dir is at the repo root (single workspace,
          # post-monorepo). Bundles live under target/<triple>/release/bundle/.
          path: |
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/dmg/*.dmg
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/macos/*.app.tar.gz
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/macos/*.app.tar.gz.sig
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/appimage/*.AppImage
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/appimage/*.AppImage.sig
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/deb/*.deb
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/msi/*.msi
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/msi/*.msi.sig
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/nsis/*.exe
            target/${{ matrix.platform.target }}/release/bundle/nsis/*.exe.sig
          # Fail loudly — a green build with no installers attached is the worst
          # failure mode (it silently produces an empty draft Release).
          if-no-files-found: error

  publish:
    name: publish to GitHub Release
    needs: build
    # Decoupled from per-leg success: run as long as the workflow wasn't
    # cancelled, so a FAILED build leg (e.g. the self-hosted Intel runner is
    # down, or x86_64 hits a compile error) still ships the arm64 + Linux
    # artifacts instead of blocking the entire release — the exact footgun
    # macos-13 created when publish was `needs: build` with implicit success().
    # The flatten step below hard-fails if NO artifacts arrived at all, so a
    # total build failure can't silently publish an empty draft.
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          # Build the TAG when called by release.yml's bump flow (the run's
          # own SHA predates the bump commit). Empty on tag pushes → default.
          ref: ${{ inputs.tag }}

      - name: Resolve tag
        id: resolve
        shell: bash
        run: |
          # Prefer explicit workflow_dispatch input. Otherwise we must be
          # on a tag push — `refs/tags/desktop-vX.Y.Z`. A dispatch on a
          # BRANCH with no tag input is a supported BUILD-ONLY run (cache
          # seeding / leg validation): skip publishing instead of failing
          # after 1.5h of green builds — the installers stay downloadable
          # as workflow-run artifacts. A malformed tag is still a hard
          # error (we'd otherwise create a Release tagged `main`).
          tag="${{ inputs.tag }}"
          if [[ -z "$tag" ]]; then
            if [[ "$GITHUB_REF" != refs/tags/* ]]; then
              echo "skip=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
              echo "::notice::No tag input and ref is not a tag ($GITHUB_REF) — build-only run; skipping the GitHub Release. Artifacts are attached to this workflow run; re-dispatch with the tag input set to publish."
              echo "### Build-only run — no Release published (no tag input; ref $GITHUB_REF). Artifacts are on this run's page." >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
              exit 0
            fi
            tag="${GITHUB_REF##refs/tags/}"
          fi
          if [[ "$tag" != desktop-v* ]]; then
            echo "::error::Tag '$tag' does not match desktop-v* pattern." >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "skip=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "tag=$tag" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Download all build artifacts
        if: steps.resolve.outputs.skip != 'true'
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: artifacts

      - name: Flatten artifact tree
        if: steps.resolve.outputs.skip != 'true'
        run: |
          mkdir -p release-assets
          # Each artifact dir is `desktop-<platform-name>/...`. Flatten
          # everything into a single dir for upload. .sig files are the
          # updater signatures that svrnme.sh/api/desktop/updater fetches
          # into the manifest — they MUST land in the release alongside
          # the artifact they sign or the updater will 404 from the
          # manifest endpoint.
          find artifacts -type f \
            \( -name "*.dmg" -o -name "*.AppImage" -o -name "*.deb" \
               -o -name "*.msi" -o -name "*.exe" -o -name "*.app.tar.gz" \
               -o -name "*.sig" \) \
            -exec cp {} release-assets/ \;
          ls -la release-assets
          # Since publish now runs even when a build leg failed (if: !cancelled()),
          # guard against the degenerate case where EVERY leg failed and we'd
          # otherwise publish an empty draft. At least one installer must exist.
          if [ -z "$(ls -A release-assets 2>/dev/null)" ]; then
            echo "::error::No build artifacts arrived — every build leg failed or uploaded nothing. Refusing to publish an empty release." >&2
            exit 1
          fi

      - name: Publish draft release
        if: steps.resolve.outputs.skip != 'true'
        uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        with:
          tag_name: ${{ steps.resolve.outputs.tag }}
          name: Sovereign Desktop ${{ steps.resolve.outputs.tag }}
          draft: true
          generate_release_notes: true
          files: release-assets/*
          body: |
            Unsigned MVP release. macOS users: right-click → Open the first time
            (Gatekeeper will warn). Windows users: SmartScreen will warn — click
            "More info" → "Run anyway".

            Auto-updates are wired: future releases will surface in-app via
            the "Check for updates" affordance, served from svrnme.sh.

            Code signing (Apple Developer ID, Windows Authenticode) is
            deferred — see `sovereign/crates/sovereign-desktop/RELEASING.md`.

        "answer": "From the retrieved sources, here is what can be established:\n\nThe problem of evil is the philosophical question of how to reconcile the existence of evil and suffering with an omnipotent, omnibenevolent, and omniscient God [Source: Problem of evil]. It sits at the intersection of philosophy of religion, theology, and ethics [Source: Problem of evil], though it also appears in secular ethics and evolutionary biology [Source: Problem of evil].\n\n### Formulations of the Problem\nThe best-known presentation of the problem is attributed to the Greek philosopher Epicurus, and was later popularized by David Hume [Source: Problem of evil]. \n\nIn contemporary terms, philosophers distinguish between different formulations. Medieval philosophers did not engage what present-day terminology calls the \"evidential\" or \"atheistic\" problems; rather, they engaged the \"aporetic\" problem of evil, attempting to resolve apparent logical incompatibilities given that natural theology had already demonstrated God's existence [Source: leibniz-evil]. The modern debate focuses heavily on two main types: the **logical** problem (arguing that God's attributes are logically incompatible with evil) and the **evidential** problem (arguing that the amount and type of suffering in the world make God's existence improbable) [Source: Christian theology].\n\nEvil itself is often categorized into moral evil (resulting from human agency) and natural evil (the result of natural causes, such as a child suffering from disease or casualties from a volcano) [Source: Problem of evil]. A major challenge to defenses based on free will is explaining why an all-powerful God would tolerate natural evils, which have no apparent connection to human free will [Source: Problem of evil]. Some authors argue against this distinction; Patricia A. Williams contends that differentiating between moral and natural evil is unjustified because \"human beings and their...\" are deeply connected to the natural world [Source: Problem of evil].\n\n### Responses: Defenses vs. Theodicies\nResponses to the problem are generally classified into total refutations, **defenses**, and **theodicies** [Source: evil], though exact definitions vary among authors [Source: Christian theology]. \n\n*   **Defenses:** Generally attempt to show there is no logical incompatibility between God's existence and evil\u2014essentially proving that a plausible explanation for why God might allow evil exists [Source: Christian theology]. A defense does not need to be proven true or highly probable; it only needs to demonstrate logical possibility [Source: Christian theology]. \n*   **Theodicies:** Are more ambitious attempts to provide a plausible justification for the existence of evil. They aim to answer the evidential problem by offering reasons that are likely true, rather than just logically possible [Source: Christian theology]. Richard Swinburne argues that one cannot assume \"greater goods\" exist unless we have a successful theodicy explaining what those goods actually are [Source: Christian theology].\n\n### Key Figures and Specific Arguments\n**Epicurus and David Hume** provided early formulations of the conflict between divine attributes and worldly suffering [Source: Problem of evil]. \n\n**Clement of Alexandria (2nd century)** proposed an early version known as the **privation theory of evil**. This theory describes evil not as a positive entity created by God, but as a negative\u2014a form of \"lack, loss or privation.\" Clement argued that because God is completely good, He could not create something that does not truly exist; therefore, evil exists only as a lack of good. However, this view was criticized for its inability to adequately explain physical suffering in the world [Source: Problem of evil].\n\n**J.L. Mackie** famously debated the logical validity of defenses against the problem of evil alongside Alvin Plantinga and Antony Flew [Source: Philosophy of religion]. \n\n**Alvin Plantinga** developed the **Free Will Defense**, which sought to show that the logical problem of evil was invalid by demonstrating that preserving free will provides a logically possible reason for God's existence despite evil [Source: Existence of God]. His defense has received strong support among academic philosophers, with many agreeing it defeated the logical formulation of the argument from evil [Source: Existence of God]. Contemporary atheologians have since attempted to add further premises to create explicitly contradictory sets involving these propositions [Source: Existence of God].\n\nIn Christian theology, several specific frameworks address the issue. The **Cruciform theodicy** is described as a thematic trajectory rather than a full system like Soul-making or Process theodicies; historically and currently, it remains the primary Christian response [Source: Problem of evil]. In this view, God is not distant but identifies Himself \"with the suffering of the world\" through Jesus\u2014a concept articulated by James Cone regarding divine solidarity with sufferers [Source: Problem of evil].         "answer": "From the retrieved sources, here is what can be established:\n\nCommon knowledge is a concept in logic and the theory of rationality that describes information shared by all agents, where each agent knows it, knows that everyone else knows it, knows that they know it, and so on ad infinitum. It serves as a foundational assumption in game theory, epistemic logic, philosophy, and computer science for modeling how groups coordinate, reach agreements, or fail to do so based on their informational states.\n\n### Definition and Intuition\nThe intuitive definition of common knowledge was introduced by David Lewis (1969), who described $p$ being common knowledge if [unverified excerpt: everyone knows $p$, everyone knows that everyone knows $p$, etc.] [Source: convention]. This infinite hierarchy distinguishes common knowledge from mutual knowledge (where everyone simply knows the fact). \n\nA classic illustration is the **Muddy Children Puzzle** (or variants like the Blue-Eyed Islanders puzzle): a group of people with blue eyes must deduce their own eye color based solely on public announcements and observing others, demonstrating how iterative reasoning about what others know leads to collective action. The puzzle highlights that without a public announcement establishing *common* knowledge, even universally true facts may not trigger coordinated behavior [Source: Common knowledge (logic)].\n\n### Formal Treatments\nSeveral formal frameworks have been developed to capture this concept rigorously:\n\n1.  **Epistemic Logic**: In multi-agent epistemic logic, adding a common knowledge operator $C$ extends expressive power. When combined with Public Announcement Logic (PAL), it forms PAC (Public Announcement Logic with Common Knowledge). The relationship between announcements and common knowledge is governed by specific rules in the logic [Source: logic-information]. \n2.  **Aumann Structures (Semantic Approach)**: Robert Aumann provided a mathematical formulation using partitions of states. If each agent has a partition representing their information, an event $E$ is common knowledge at state $s$ if there exists a subset of states containing $s$, contained within every agent's cell that contains $s$. Formally, this can be defined as $C(e) = \\bigcap_{n=1}^{\\infty} E^n(e)$ [Source: Common knowledge (logic)]. This semantic approach corresponds to syntactic Kripke structures where accessibility relations define equivalence classes based on agents' partitions [Source: Common knowledge (logic)].\n3.  **Alternative Analyses**: Stephen Schiffer and others have offered different formalizations of Lewis\u2019s informal remarks, leading to ongoing scholarly debate about the precise relation between these later mathematical models and Lewis\u2019s original philosophical intent [Source: convention].\n\n### Key Results in Game Theory and Rationality\nCommon knowledge plays a central role in epistemic game theory, though its necessity has been refined over time:\n\n*   **Iterated Elimination of Dominated Strategies**: A central result states that \"rationality and common belief in rationality implies iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies\" [Source: epistemic-game]. This highlights how higher-order information (knowing what others know) drives strategic reasoning.\n*   **Nash Equilibrium Conditions**: It was long assumed that *common knowledge of rationality* among players is fundamental for Nash equilibrium. However, Aumann and Brandenburger (1995) demonstrated that in two-player games, common knowledge of rationality is actually *not needed* as an epistemic condition to derive Nash equilibrium strategies; mutual belief suffices under certain conditions [Source: Common knowledge (logic)]. \n    *   *Correction*: Contrary to some earlier beliefs, the sources clarify that [unverified excerpt: Common knowledge of rationality is neither necessary nor sufficient for Nash Equilibrium] [Source: epistemic-game].\n*   **No-Trade Theorems**: Milgrom\u2019s work shows that given specific conditions on market efficiency and information, speculative trade between rational agents is impossible if prices reflect common knowledge. This result links informational structures directly to economic outcomes [Source: Common knowledge (logic)].\n\n### Applications Across Disciplines\n1.  **Game Theory**: As noted by von Neumann and Morgenstern (1944) and subsequent literature, assumptions about common knowledge are crucial in modeling strategic interactions where actions depend heavily on what players know about each other's knowledge [Source: common-knowledge].\n2.  **Computer Science & Distributed Systems**: Computer scientists use epistemic logics incorporating common knowledge to reason about distributed algorithms, consensus protocols, and multi-agent systems. It helps verify whether agents can coordinate despite partial information or communication failures [Source: Common knowledge (logic)].\n3.  **Fair Division Protocols**: In social procedures like cake-cutting, issues of knowledge and ignorance are critical.         "answer": "From the retrieved sources, here is what can be established:\n\nCommon knowledge is a concept in logic and the theory of rationality that describes information shared by all agents, where each agent knows it, knows that everyone else knows it, knows that they know it, and so on ad infinitum. It serves as a foundational assumption in game theory, epistemic logic, philosophy, and computer science for modeling how groups coordinate, reach agreements, or fail to do so based on their informational states.\n\n### Definition and Intuition\nThe intuitive definition of common knowledge was introduced by David Lewis (1969), who described $p$ being common knowledge if [unverified excerpt: everyone knows $p$, everyone knows that everyone knows $p$, etc.] [Source: convention]. This infinite hierarchy distinguishes common knowledge from mutual knowledge (where everyone simply knows the fact). \n\nA classic illustration is the **Muddy Children Puzzle** (or variants like the Blue-Eyed Islanders puzzle): a group of people with blue eyes must deduce their own eye color based solely on public announcements and observing others, demonstrating how iterative reasoning about what others know leads to collective action. The puzzle highlights that without a public announcement establishing *common* knowledge, even universally true facts may not trigger coordinated behavior [Source: Common knowledge (logic)].\n\n### Formal Treatments\nSeveral formal frameworks have been developed to capture this concept rigorously:\n\n1.  **Epistemic Logic**: In multi-agent epistemic logic, adding a common knowledge operator $C$ extends expressive power. When combined with Public Announcement Logic (PAL), it forms PAC (Public Announcement Logic with Common Knowledge). The relationship between announcements and common knowledge is governed by specific rules in the logic [Source: logic-information]. \n2.  **Aumann Structures (Semantic Approach)**: Robert Aumann provided a mathematical formulation using partitions of states. If each agent has a partition representing their information, an event $E$ is common knowledge at state $s$ if there exists a subset of states containing $s$, contained within every agent's cell that contains $s$. Formally, this can be defined as $C(e) = \\bigcap_{n=1}^{\\infty} E^n(e)$ [Source: Common knowledge (logic)]. This semantic approach corresponds to syntactic Kripke structures where accessibility relations define equivalence classes based on agents' partitions [Source: Common knowledge (logic)].\n3.  **Alternative Analyses**: Stephen Schiffer and others have offered different formalizations of Lewis\u2019s informal remarks, leading to ongoing scholarly debate about the precise relation between these later mathematical models and Lewis\u2019s original philosophical intent [Source: convention].\n\n### Key Results in Game Theory and Rationality\nCommon knowledge plays a central role in epistemic game theory, though its necessity has been refined over time:\n\n*   **Iterated Elimination of Dominated Strategies**: A central result states that \"rationality and common belief in rationality implies iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies\" [Source: epistemic-game]. This highlights how higher-order information (knowing what others know) drives strategic reasoning.\n*   **Nash Equilibrium Conditions**: It was long assumed that *common knowledge of rationality* among players is fundamental for Nash equilibrium. However, Aumann and Brandenburger (1995) demonstrated that in two-player games, common knowledge of rationality is actually *not needed* as an epistemic condition to derive Nash equilibrium strategies; mutual belief suffices under certain conditions [Source: Common knowledge (logic)]. \n    *   *Correction*: Contrary to some earlier beliefs, the sources clarify that [unverified excerpt: Common knowledge of rationality is neither necessary nor sufficient for Nash Equilibrium] [Source: epistemic-game].\n*   **No-Trade Theorems**: Milgrom\u2019s work shows that given specific conditions on market efficiency and information, speculative trade between rational agents is impossible if prices reflect common knowledge.         "answer": "# Idealism: A Comprehensive Overview\n\nIdealism is a broad family of philosophical positions that, in its strongest form, asserts that reality is fundamentally mental or spiritual. While the term has been used loosely to describe various doctrines (including Platonism and certain theological views), modern idealism—particularly as it crystallized in the 18th and 19th centuries—is defined by specific epistemological and ontological claims about the relationship between mind, thought, and being [Source: idealism].\n\n### Central Claims\nThe core thesis of idealism can be summarized as follows: **reality is not independent of consciousness.** Unlike materialists, who argue that matter exists independently of observers, idealists contend that what we call \"the world\" is either constituted by minds or dependent on mental structures for its existence.\n\nIdealism generally distinguishes itself from skepticism (which doubts our knowledge of an external world) by claiming to offer a more robust account of reality. Idealists often argue that because all experience is mediated through categories of understanding (such as space, time, and causality), the very notion of a \"thing-in-itself\" existing outside these frameworks is incoherent [Source: idealism]. Thus, to be is to be perceived (*esse est percipi*) or to be thought.\n\n### Major Varieties and Figures\nScholars typically divide modern idealism into two main branches based on their starting points: **Subjective** and **Objective**.\n\n#### 1. Subjective Idealism\nThis form begins with the individual mind. It argues that objects only exist insofar as they are perceived by finite minds.\n*   **George Berkeley (1685–1753):** The most famous proponent of subjective idealism. Berkeley argued against John Locke’s distinction between primary qualities (objective) and secondary qualities (subjective). He claimed all qualities are subjective, leading him to conclude that material substance is an unnecessary hypothesis. For Berkeley, God sustains the existence of objects when no human is perceiving them [Source: Idealism].\n*   **Christian Wolff:** Although not a \"idealist\" in the modern sense, he coined the term \"idealism\" in the early 18th century to describe views that prioritized mental representations over external reality [Source: Idealism].\n\n#### 2. Objective Idealism\nThis form argues that there exists a single, universal mind or rational structure underlying all reality. Individual minds participate in this greater consciousness.\n*   **Immanuel Kant (1724–1804):** Often seen as the bridge between empiricism and idealism. While Kant was a \"transcendental idealist,\" he did not deny the existence of things-in-themselves (*noumena*). Instead, he argued that we can only know phenomena (things as they appear) because our minds impose structures like space and time on sensory data [Source: Argumentation theory; Source: idealism].\n*   **G.W.F. Hegel (1770–1831):** The towering figure of German Idealism. For Hegel, reality is *Geist* (Spirit/Mind). History is the process by which Spirit comes to know itself. He rejected the dualism between subject and object, arguing instead for a dialectical unity where thought and being are identical in their ultimate rational structure [Source: German idealism].\n*   **Friedrich Schleiermacher:** A theologian who asserted that the ideal (mental activity) and the real (physical nature) are united in God, though they do not causally affect one another [Source: German idealism].\n\n#### 3. British Absolute Idealism\nIn the late 19th century, idealism became the dominant metaphysics in the English-speaking world before being challenged by analytic philosophy.\n*   **Francis Herbert Bradley:** Argued that relations are inherently contradictory if taken as ultimately real. He posited an \"Absolute\" which is a single, all-inclusive experience where diversity is harmonized but not fundamentally separate [Source: Idealism].\n*   **J.M.E. McTaggart:** Broke from the monistic trend to defend pluralistic idealism, arguing that reality consists of a multiplicity of spirits related harmoniously through love [Source: Idealism].\n\n### Principal Arguments for Idealism\n1.  **The Argument from Perception (Berkeley):** We never perceive matter directly; we only perceive ideas/sensations. Therefore, it is more parsimonious to say objects *are* collections of sensations rather than mysterious substrates causing them.\n2.  **The Transcendental Argument (Kant/Hegel):** Space, time, and logical categories are not features of the world \"out there\" but conditions necessary for any experience to occur. Since we cannot conceive of an object without these forms, reality as such must be structured by mind-like properties [Source: idealism].\n3.  **The Coherence Theory of Truth:** Idealists often argue that truth is a property of systems of beliefs or experiences rather than isolated propositions matching external facts. This supports the view that reality is a unified mental whole (the Absolute) rather than a collection of disjointed material atoms [Source: Idealism].\n\n### Main Lines of Criticism\nIdealism faced severe criticism in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, leading to its decline in Anglo-American philosophy.\n\n#### 1. The Common Sense / Realist Reaction\n*   **G.E. Moore and Bertrand Russell:** These philosophers argued that idealism confused the *act* of thinking with the *object* thought about. They asserted that tables and chairs exist independently of whether anyone is looking at them. Russell famously championed \"logical atomism,\" positing that reality consists of simple, independent facts rather than a unified whole [Source: Argumentation theory].\n*   **J.L. Austin:** Criticized idealism for relying on flawed concepts of universals and language. He argued that idealists misinterpreted linguistic structures (like using one word for many instances) as evidence for metaphysical unities [Source: J. L. Austin].\n\n#### 2. The Rejection of the Absolute\nCritics argued that Hegel’s Absolute was incoherent because it tried to include everything—including contradictions—within itself. Critics like McTaggart noted that even within idealist circles, explaining individual freedom became difficult if all is part of a single Spirit [Source: Idealism].\n\n#### 3. Scientific Materialism and Evolutionary Theory\nThe rise of Darwinian biology suggested that mind evolved from non-conscious matter over billions of years, reversing the idealist claim that matter depends on mind. This empirical evidence made materialism more attractive to scientists and many philosophers [Source: Argumentation theory].\n\n### Current Status\nBy the mid-20th century, explicit defenses of idealism were rare in Anglophone philosophy due to the dominance of analytic methods which prioritize linguistic clarity and scientific naturalism [Source: idealism].         "answer": "A comprehensive overview of the cosmological argument for the existence of God.\n\n### Overview and Definition\nThe **cosmological argument** is a class of *a posteriori* arguments in natural theology that asserts the existence of God can be inferred from facts concerning causation, explanation, change, motion, contingency, dependency, or finitude with respect to the universe [Source: Cosmological argument]. Often referred to as an \"argument from first cause,\" \"prime mover argument,\" or \"universal causation\" [Source: Cosmological argument], it posits that there must be a foundational reason or entity responsible for all existence [Source: Existence]. The basic premises involve the concept of causation, leading to the conclusion that a \"first cause\" exists, which is subsequently analyzed and identified as God [Source: Cosmological argument].\n\n### Historical Development\nThe history of this line of reasoning traces back to **Aristotle** (or earlier), was developed in Neoplatonism and early Christianity, and later flourished in medieval Islamic theology during the 9th to 12th centuries [Source: Cosmological argument; Source: Cosmological argument]. In Christian philosophy, it was re-introduced by **Thomas Aquinas** in the 13th century [Source: Cosmological argument]. \n\nIn Islamic philosophy, **Avicenna** formulated a highly influential version known as the \"Proof of the Truthful\" (*wajib al-wujud*), arguing that there must be an entity that cannot not exist. Historian Peter Adamson has called this Avicenna's biggest contribution to the history of philosophy [Source: Avicenna]. The argument is also closely related to the principle of sufficient reason, addressed by **Gottfried Leibniz** and Samuel Clarke, which modernizes the claim attributed to Parmenides that \"nothing comes from nothing\" [Source: Cosmological argument].\n\n### Major Forms of the Argument\nScholars generally distinguish between two basic variants based on subtle but important distinctions: *in esse* (essentiality) and *in fieri* (becoming) [Source: Cosmological argument]. \n\n1.  **The Kalam Cosmological Argument:** This form contends for a first or beginning cause of the universe and has a venerable history in Islamic theology (*mutakalliman tradition*) [Source: cosmological-argument; Source: cosmological-argument]. It asserts that since everything that begins to exist has a cause, and the universe began to exist, the universe must have had an uncaused cause identified as God. Contemporary Christian apologist **William Lane Craig** is its most prominent defender, marshaling multidisciplinary evidence for its premises [Source: Existence of God; Source: cosmological-argument].\n2.  **The Contingency Argument (Leibnizian):** This form focuses on why anything exists at all rather than just how it came into being. Modern variations include those by **Richard Swinburne**, who argues the argument is not deductively valid but probabilistic [Source: cosmological-argument]; **Robert Koons**, who uses mereology and modal logic to take a \"new look\" at contingency [Source: cosmological-argument]; and versions proposed by **Richard Gale** and **Alexander Pruss** based on a weak principle of sufficient reason, or by Michael Almeida using modal realism [Source: cosmological-argument].\n\n### Principal Figures\n*   **Aristotle:** Early proponent of arguments regarding motion and causation.\n*   **Avicenna (Ibn Sina):** Formulated the *Proof of the Truthful*.\n*   **Thomas Aquinas:** Re-introduced and systematized these arguments in medieval Christian theology.\n*   **Gottfried Leibniz & Samuel Clarke:** Developed versions relying heavily on the Principle of Sufficient Reason.\n*   **William Lane Craig:** The leading contemporary defender of the Kalam argument.\n*   **Richard Swinburne, Robert Koons, Richard Gale, Alexander Pruss, Michael Almeida:** Key figures in modern analytic philosophy refining or critiquing contingency-based cosmological arguments [Source: cosmological-argument].\n\n### Principal Objections\nCritics have objected to key premises across historical and contemporary iterations [Source: cosmological-argument; Source: natural-theology]:\n\n1.  **The \"Gap\" Problem (Attributes):** A major objection is that even if a first cause exists, it does not necessarily possess the attributes of theistic God—such as omniscience, omnipotence, and omnibenevolence [Source: Cosmological argument]. The argument may only establish a cosmic architect rather than a personal deity. Defenders often expand the conclusion to assert these attributes are necessary truths of such a being [Source: Cosmological argument].\n2.  **Infinite Regress vs. First Cause:** Critics question whether an infinite regress of causes is logically impossible or merely counterintuitive. If every effect has a cause, why must there be one uncaused cause? \n3.  **The Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR):** Objections target the PSR itself—the idea that everything must have a sufficient reason for its existence. Some argue this principle cannot be applied to the universe as a whole in the same way it applies to parts within it.\n4.  **Evolutionary/Imperfection Arguments:** While often directed at design arguments, some objections based on evolution—such as the \"argument from imperfection\" regarding vestigial organs or suffering—are raised against theistic creation generally [Source: Existence of God].\n\n### Conclusion and Limitations\nThe cosmological argument remains one of the most enduring frameworks in natural theology, evolving from ancient metaphysics into complex modern analytic philosophy involving modal logic and mereology [Source: Cosmological argument; Source: cosmological-argument]. \n\n*Note: The provided knowledge base contains significant gaps regarding specific historical counter-arguments (e.g., Hume's specific critiques) and detailed logical formalizations.         "answer": "# The Problem of Evil in the Philosophy of Religion\n\nThe problem of evil is one of the most enduring and significant challenges within the philosophy of religion.         "answer": "René Descartes (1596–1650) is widely regarded as the father of modern Western philosophy, primarily for shifting the philosophical focus from \"what is true\" to \"of what can I be certain?\" [Source: René Descartes]. His epistemology is a rigorous attempt to establish an indubitable foundation for all human knowledge. This overview covers his methodological doubt, foundational certainties, the role of God in securing that certainty, and the principal difficulties raised by critics.\n\n### 1. The Method of Radical Doubt\nDescartes’ primary tool for establishing certainty is **methodical doubt** (or hyperbolic doubt). In *Meditations on First Philosophy* (1641), he aims to refute skepticism once and for all by entertaining the widest and most radical doubts possible [Source: malebranche-ideas; Source: René Descartes]. \n\nHe challenges his own reasoning and reason itself, systematically doubting any belief that can be doubted even slightly [Source: Discourse on the Method]. This includes:\n*   **Sensory Illusion:** Since our senses have deceived us in the past (e.g., optical illusions), we cannot trust them completely.\n*   **The Dream Argument:** There is no definitive mark by which to distinguish waking life from dreaming; thus, sense experience is dubitable [Source: Rationalism].\n*   **The Evil Demon Hypothesis:** Descartes entertains the possibility of a powerful, malicious demon who is systematically deceiving him about everything he perceives or thinks [Source: descartes-epistemology context implies this radical doubt phase].\n\nThis method strips away all beliefs based on authority, tradition, and sensory experience to see what remains when every possible ground for doubt has been exhausted.\n\n### 2. Foundational Certainties: The Cogito\nFrom this abyss of doubt, Descartes identifies one truth that cannot be doubted: **\"I think, therefore I am\"** (*cogito, ergo sum*) [Source: Discourse on the Method; Source: René Descartes]. \n\n*   **The Nature of the Self:** Even if an evil demon is deceiving him about everything else, he must exist in order to be deceived or to doubt. As Descartes writes, \"He cannot doubt that something has to be there to do the doubting\" [Source: Discourse on the Method]. \n*   **Mind-Body Distinction:** This certainty leads to a dualistic epistemology where the mind (res cogitans) is known more clearly and distinctly than the body (res extensa). In the Second Meditation, reflecting on his position regarding himself and the famous \"wax argument,\" Descartes establishes that knowledge comes from intellectual intuition rather than sensory perception alone [Source: descartes-epistemology].\n\nDescartes argues that only knowledge of eternal truths—such as those in mathematics and logic—can be attained by reason alone. Other knowledge requires experience aided by the scientific method [Source: Rationalism]. His first rule of thought was never to accept anything for true which he did not know to be such; specifically, nothing should be included in judgment unless it is presented so clearly and distinctly as to exclude all ground of doubt [Source: René Descartes].\n\n### 3. The Role of God\nThe *Cogito* establishes the existence of the self but does not yet guarantee knowledge of the external world or mathematical truths.         "answer": "John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) was the most influential English-speaking philosopher of the nineteenth century and a central figure in classical liberalism [Source: John Stuart Mill]. A naturalist, empiricist, utilitarian, and liberal, his work sought to synthesize eighteenth-century Enlightenment rationalism with nineteenth-century Romantic and historical sensibilities [Source: mill]. He is widely recognized for transforming Jeremy Bentham’s rigid utilitarian framework into a more nuanced ethical system that placed high value on individual liberty, intellectual diversity, and social progress [Source: mill-moral-political; Source: bentham].\n\n### Utilitarian Moral Philosophy\nMill's moral philosophy is grounded in **utilitarianism**, an ethical theory he inherited from his father James Mill and the radical reformer Jeremy Bentham. While Bentham viewed human motivation through a strictly quantitative lens—calculating pleasure against pain based solely on intensity and duration—Mill introduced qualitative distinctions to address criticisms of \"philosophical hedonism\" as a doctrine worthy only of swine [Source: bentham; Source: Meaning of life]. \n\nIn his seminal work *Utilitarianism* (1863), originally published as articles in 1861, Mill argued that some kinds of pleasures are intrinsically more valuable than others because they engage our higher faculties [Source: Utilitarianism]. He famously asserted it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. For Mill, the ultimate standard of morality was the **Greatest Happiness Principle**: actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness (pleasure and the absence of pain) and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse [Source: Meaning of life; Source: John Stuart Mill]. However, he expanded this concept beyond mere physical gratification to include intellectual, emotional, and moral satisfactions, arguing that human beings possess \"permanent interests\" as progressive social creatures [Source: John Stuart Mill].\n\n### Political Principles\nMill’s political philosophy is defined by his rigorous defense of individual liberty against both state tyranny and the \"tyranny of the majority.\" He believed that a democratic society could only remain free if it strictly adhered to limits on legitimate power.\n\n**The Harm Principle:** In *On Liberty* (1859), Mill articulated what has become known as the **Principle of Liberty**. He stated that \"the sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their members... is self-protection\" [Source: John Stuart Mill]. This means that society may only coerce an individual against their will to prevent harm to others; matters concerning only oneself—whether physical or moral—are inviolable. \n\nMill championed absolute freedom of speech and thought, arguing that silencing an opinion robs humanity by assuming our own infallibility. Even false opinions must be tolerated because truth emerges strongest when tested through open debate [Source: mill-moral-political].\n\n**Representative Government:** In *Considerations on Representative Government* (1861), Mill advocated for a democratic system but with safeguards against the incompetence of the masses. He supported universal suffrage in principle but proposed plural voting rights for the educated elite to balance popular rule with wisdom [Source: mill-moral-political]. He also emphasized the importance of local self-government as a school for civic virtue.\n\n### Feminism and Social Reform\nMill was an early feminist whose work laid foundational stones for liberal feminism. His collaboration with his second wife, **Harriet Taylor Mill**, culminated in *The Subjection of Women* (published posthumously in 1869). The book argued that legal inequality between men and women was a relic of barbarous times and fundamentally unjust [Source: John Stuart Mill; Source: harriet-mill]. \n\nHistorically significant, Mill became the first member of Parliament to call explicitly for women's suffrage since Henry Hunt did so in 1832 [Source: John Stuart Mill]. He viewed the subordination of women as one of the greatest hindrances to human improvement, arguing that equality would unleash half of humanity’s intellectual potential.\n\n### Major Works\nMill produced an extensive body of work across logic, ethics, politics, and economics. His most enduring texts include:\n*   ***A System of Logic*** **(1843):** A foundational text on empiricism and scientific methodology, establishing how we derive knowledge from experience through induction rather than pure deduction [Source: mill; Source: mill-moral-political].\n*   ***On Liberty*** **(1859):** The definitive defense of free speech and individual autonomy against social conformity and state overreach [Source: John Stuart Mill].\n*   ***Utilitarianism*** **(1863):** His mature articulation of the Greatest Happiness Principle, distinguishing between higher and lower pleasures [Source: Utilitarianism].\n*   ***Principles of Political Economy*** **(1848):** An influential economic treatise that blended classical economics with socialist-leaning reforms regarding wealth distribution [Source: mill-moral-political].\n\n### Conclusion\nJohn Stuart Mill remains a towering figure in moral and political philosophy. By refining utilitarianism to account for human dignity and by establishing robust philosophical defenses for civil liberties, he shaped modern liberal democracy. While his specific policy proposals have evolved over time, his core insistence on individual autonomy, intellectual freedom, and social progress continues to define the boundaries of public discourse today.",

        "answer": "# Conservatism as a Political Philosophy: A Comprehensive Overview\n\nConservatism is one of the most significant political ideologies in modern history, characterized by its emphasis on tradition, social stability, and gradual change. Unlike liberalism or socialism, which often begin with abstract theories about how society *should* be organized based on reason or equality, conservatism tends to view society as an organic entity that has evolved over time through custom, habit, and historical experience. This fundamental difference shapes its central commitments, its principal theorists, and its relationship with rival traditions.\n\n## Central Commitments\n\nAt its core, conservatism holds several key beliefs that distinguish it from other political philosophies:\n\n1. **Tradition and Custom**: Conservatives believe that long-standing institutions, customs, and practices embody the accumulated wisdom of generations. These \"prejudices\" (in Edmund Burke's sense) are not irrational biases but tested solutions to social problems [Source: conservatism]. Tradition provides a framework for understanding one’s place in the world and offers stability in an uncertain environment.\n\n2. **Skepticism of Abstract Reason**: Conservatism is deeply suspicious of attempts to redesign society based on pure reason or utopian blueprints. It argues that human beings are complex, imperfect creatures whose behavior cannot be fully predicted or controlled by theoretical models. This skepticism leads conservatives to favor incremental reform over radical revolution [Source: conservatism].\n\n3. **Organic Society**: Conservatives view society as an organic whole, composed of interdependent parts such as family, community, religion, and nation. These institutions are seen as natural outgrowths of human nature rather than artificial constructs designed by rational planning. The health of the whole depends on the strength of its constituent parts [Source: conservatism].\n\n4. **Hierarchy and Authority**: While not all conservatives advocate for rigid social hierarchies, most accept that some form of authority is necessary for social order. This can manifest in support for traditional leadership structures, respect for established institutions (such as monarchy or church), and a belief that inequality is sometimes natural or beneficial [Source: conservatism].\n\n5. **Property and Economic Order**: Conservatives generally defend private property rights and free markets, seeing them as essential to individual liberty and social stability. However, unlike classical liberals who may prioritize economic efficiency above all else, conservatives often emphasize the moral and communal dimensions of economic life, warning against the corrosive effects of unchecked capitalism on family and community bonds [Source: Liberal conservatism].\n\n6. **Religion and Morality**: Many conservative traditions place great importance on religion as a source of moral guidance and social cohesion. While not all conservatives are religious, most believe that shared moral values—often rooted in religious tradition—are necessary for maintaining social order and preventing moral relativism or nihilism [Source: conservatism].\n\n7. **National Identity and Sovereignty**: Conservatives tend to emphasize the importance of national identity, culture, and sovereignty. They view nations as communities with shared histories, languages, and customs that should be protected from external influences or supranational entities that might undermine local autonomy [Source: conservatism].\n\n## Principal Theorists\n\nConservatism has been shaped by several key thinkers who have articulated its principles in different historical contexts:\n\n### Edmund Burke (1729–1797)\nOften regarded as the father of modern conservatism, Burke was an Irish-born British statesman and philosopher whose *Reflections on the Revolution in France* (1750) remains a foundational text. Burke argued against the French Revolution’s attempt to dismantle existing institutions based on abstract notions of liberty and equality. He emphasized the importance of gradual reform, respect for tradition, and the dangers of radical change driven by ideological fervor [Source: conservatism]. For Burke, society is a partnership \"between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born,\" implying that we have obligations to both our ancestors and future generations.\n\n### Friedrich Hayek (1899–1992)\nAlthough often associated with classical liberalism or libertarianism, Hayek made significant contributions to conservative thought through his critique of central planning and socialism. In *The Road to Serfdom* (1944), he argued that economic planning inevitably leads to political tyranny because it concentrates power in the hands of a few planners. Hayek emphasized the role of spontaneous order—the idea that complex social systems emerge naturally from individual actions rather than being designed by rational authorities [Source: Liberal conservatism]. His work influenced many modern conservatives who advocate for free markets and limited government intervention.\n\n### Michael Oakeshott (1901–1990)\nAn English philosopher known for his skeptical approach to politics, Oakeshott distinguished between \"rationalism\" and \"practical knowledge.\" He criticized the belief that politics can be reduced to technical problems solvable through scientific methods or ideological doctrines. Instead, he viewed political life as a matter of navigating traditions and customs without expecting definitive solutions. Oakeshott’s essay *Rationalism in Politics* argues against the idea that society should be organized according to preconceived plans [Source: conservatism]. His thought resonates with traditionalist conservatives who value experience over theory.\n\n### Russell Kirk (1918–1994)\nAn American historian and author, Kirk is considered one of the leading figures of post-war American conservatism.
